title: Second Law holds because experiments cannot prepare randomness-decreasing states

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Second Law holds because experiments cannot prepare randomness-decreasing states

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The Second Law of Thermodynamics is observed to hold because practical experiments can only set up initial conditions that are simple to describe and construct, and finding initial conditions of a reversible system that would lead to decreasing randomness requires computation as great as the system's own evolution.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: The consequence of this is that no reasonable experiment can ever involve setting up the kind of initial conditions that will lead to decreases in randomness, and that therefore all practical experiments will tend to show only increases in randomness.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 9, “Fundamental Physics”; section “Irreversibility and the Second Law of Thermodynamics” (from p. 441), p. 444. Scope: reversible physical systems and the experiments performed on them; origin of the Second Law of Thermodynamics

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch09-04: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.46

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Specified reversible models permit direct tests linking initial-state description length to entropy behavior, and selected experiments can test reversibility and fluctuations. The general causal explanation of the Second Law uses vague practical and computational limits and competes with statistical typicality accounts. Current resources therefore resolve model-specific implications, not the universal explanation.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: In reversible simulations and controlled many-body experiments, compare entropy trajectories from initial states stratified by description and preparation complexity, and measure the computation needed to construct entropy-decreasing states. The claim predicts entropy increase for all practically preparable low-complexity states and preparation cost comparable to reverse evolution for decreases.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Observed entropy increase does not uniquely identify computational preparation limits as its cause.

Reasonable experiment and simple to describe are observer- and technology-dependent.

Entropy-decreasing fluctuations occur probabilistically in finite systems.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Entropy increase from simple initial conditions can be recomputed for reversible cellular automata and is extensively documented for gases. The explanation that this happens because finding atypical initial conditions is as hard as the evolution itself is not distinguished, by those data, from other typicality arguments. The empirical regularity is partly testable; the stated cause is not settled by existing resources.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For reversible cellular automata and for laboratory thermodynamic systems, compare entropy change from simple prepared initial conditions with the computational cost of finding initial conditions that decrease randomness. Entropy increase from every simple preparation, and no shorter search for decreasing preparations than running the dynamics, would support the account for those systems; an easy construction of randomness-decreasing states, or simple preparations whose entropy falls, would count against it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The claim that no shorter procedure exists is a general complexity statement, not a quantity tabulated for physical experiments.

A cosmological low-entropy initial condition predicts the same laboratory facts without the computational story.
